replies.author: @arildonslaught1653
replies.text:
You are only talking about "Municipal taxes" (kommunalskatt).

Most people in Sweden believe they only pay around 30–33% in tax on their salary. That number is real, but it only tells part of the story.
What most Swedes see and refer to is the municipal tax (kommunalskatt), which averages about 32.4%. For the majority of ordinary earners, this is the only income tax they pay, since they don’t reach the threshold for the additional national/state tax. That’s why many say “I only pay about 30% in tax.”
However, this figure leaves out several major components:

Employer payroll contributions — On top of your gross salary, the employer pays roughly 31.4% in social security contributions, pension fees and other payroll taxes. This is a significant hidden cost of employment.
Earned income tax credit (jobbskatteavdrag) — This credit reduces the actual income tax paid on work income, which is why many people get money back when they file their tax return. It lowers the effective rate below the headline municipal tax.
Consumption taxes — Once you receive your net salary, a large portion is taxed again when you spend it — primarily through 25% VAT (moms) on most goods and services, plus excise taxes on fuel, electricity, alcohol, tobacco, etc.

When you add together employer contributions + income tax (after the main credit) + consumption taxes, the total tax burden on a regular salary often reaches around 50% or more. This is why some people say that even ordinary salaries in Sweden carry a tax burden of about 52%. It’s not that the visible 30% is wrong — it’s just incomplete. The higher number reflects the full picture of what is ultimately paid to the public sector in connection with that income.
